form_citation: Guyton AC, Lindsey AW, Abernathy B, Richardson T. Venous return at various right atrial pressures and the normal venous return curve. Am J Physiol 1957;189:609-615.
notes: CORRECTION: an earlier version of this row said Guyton's venous return curve is 'NONLINEAR with a plateau'. That was asserted from memory and is WRONG in the load-bearing part. Guyton 1957 (12 open-chest dogs with intact reflexes, 14 areflex dogs) report venous return reaching a maximum when right atrial pressure falls to -2 to -4 mmHg and holding that maximum down to arbitrarily negative pressures, while as RAP rises to positive values VR falls linearly and reaches zero when RAP equals mean circulatory pressure. So VR is LINEAR across the whole positive-RAP operating range; the plateau is a boundary at RAP < about -2 to -4 mmHg, not general curvature. The linearisation here is therefore BETTER supported than the previous note claimed. WHAT STILL NEEDS SOURCING: this relation is CO vs blood VOLUME, not VR vs RAP. It composes volume->Pms (venous compliance) with Pms-RAP->VR (resistance). It is linear only if venous compliance is linear over the range. Guyton's own model does assume that - Beard and Feigl 2011 (10.1152/ajpheart.00228.2011) describe it as invoking a simple linear assumption that compartment volume is proportional to compliance times transmural pressure - but the compliance step should be sourced separately rather than inherited. LIVE CONTROVERSY, record it: Beard and Feigl argue Guyton's interpretation interchanges independent and dependent variables and recommend the venous return concept be removed from teaching materials.

notes: THE MODEL'S SPINE. LINEAR FORM IS NOW SOURCED AND SUPPORTED - an earlier note in this ledger asserted Guyton's curve was 'markedly nonlinear'; that was asserted from memory without checking and IS RETRACTED. Roman and Cowley 1985, rat, denervated kidney with vasopressin, aldosterone, corticosterone and noradrenaline clamped by infusion, report the relation as the slope of a LINE at 2 uL/min/kidney/mmHg over RPP 90-160 mmHg with no change in GFR, RBF or peritubular capillary pressure. Their reported 5-20 fold range and their 'doubles for 5 mmHg' are both reproduced by that single constant slope on a baseline of 7-35 uL/min, so neither implies curvature. Osborn and DiBona 1981 independently report UNaV falling LINEARLY over 137-55 mmHg in dog. VALIDITY RANGE roughly 55-160 mmHg; the model's RN.AUTOREG.UPPER of 180 sits outside the evidenced range. MAGNITUDE CROSS-CHECK: Mizelle 1993 (dog, split bladder, bilateral servo-control, 12 days - the cleanest isolation of pressure per se, since both kidneys share one neurohumoral environment) gives 3.47 mmol/day/mmHg whole-animal, which is 2.15e-4 of filtered load per mmHg against the model's 7.94e-4: the calibrated slope is 3.7x STEEPER than the animal data on a scaling-free basis. CURVATURE NOT ESTABLISHED - Mizelle's two segments differ 2.3-fold but the control point is a different day, so three points cannot separate curvature from condition. STRUCTURAL EXPOSURE, larger than the shape question: Seeliger et al. J Physiol 2004;559:939-951 servo-controlled RPP during saline loading in freely moving dogs and found NO reduction in peak or cumulative natriuresis, and Bie 2018 (10.1152/ajpregu.00363.2017) argues sodium excretion is regulated primarily by volume-keyed neurohumoral mechanisms rather than pressure.
